n: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Rosary
w: Consecrated on the Feast of the Immaculate Conception in 1900, this French Gothic revival church replaced an earlier chapel and has been likened to Chartres Cathedral. w: One of Canada's grand railway hotels, this Chateauesque pile of copper turrets opened in May 1939 in the Financial District. At 112 metres and seventeen floors it was Vancouver's tallest building for three decades, until the TD Tower overtook it in 1972 -- a long reign for a hotel built like a French chateau.

w: Long before it held art, this building was Vancouver's provincial courthouse, designed by Francis Rattenbury, now a National Historic Site. w: On June 17, 1958, a support span of this cantilever bridge collapsed mid-construction, killing a crew of ironworkers -- a disaster the finished 1960 crossing carries in its name. At 1,292 metres it still links Vancouver to the North Shore, tolled until 1963 and named, permanently, for the men who never saw it open.

w: Founded 1907 as the Vancouver Exhibition Association, this nonprofit has run a fair at Hastings Park every summer since 1910 -- a 15-day run of barns, midway rides and grandstand shows. Playland, the adjoining amusement park, folded into the group in 1993, making the PNE one of Vancouver's longest-running institutions.

w: Completed in 1930 as Vancouver's tallest building, the Marine Building wears its name literally -- terracotta seahorses, crabs and ships crawl across its facade in a full Art Deco fever dream. Ranked among the finest Deco buildings anywhere, its ornate corridors have made it a favorite backdrop for film and TV crews.

w: Vancouver's highest point, at 125 metres, used to be a basalt quarry, its stone blasted out in the early 1900s to help pave the city's early roads. When the rock ran out, the pits were reborn as gardens and lookouts -- the sunken quarry gardens still trace the shape of the holes the road-builders left behind.
